title: Copper and Courage: How a Punjabi Family Rebuilt Their Las Vegas Restaurant and Earned a James Beard Nod
excerpt: When the Dhillon family's beloved Indian restaurant was demolished with the Hawaiian Marketplace, their son brought it back — and in its first year, Tamba became a James Beard Best New Restaurant finalist.
body:
The name Tamba means "copper" in Hindi — a metal sacred in Indian tradition, believed to purify water and bring good health. For the Dhillon family, it also represents something harder to forge: the will to start over after the wrecking ball took everything.

Daljit and Jatinder Dhillon were immigrants who built their American lives in restaurant kitchens. They opened India's Clay Oven in Monterey, California, in 1989, then Gandhi India's Cuisine in 1992. When they landed in Las Vegas, they opened Tamba on the Strip — and for nearly twenty years, it became a fixture of the city's culinary and cultural life, a place where families gathered, weddings were celebrated, and Indian cuisine earned its place amid the spectacle of the world's entertainment capital.

Then, in 2022, the Hawaiian Marketplace was demolished. Tamba closed.

## A Son's Reinvention

Sunny Dhillon grew up in those kitchens, learning at his father's side for over three decades. When the original Tamba shuttered, a lesser ambition might have produced a quiet reopening somewhere off the radar. Instead, in late 2024, Dhillon brought the restaurant back at Town Square — not as a replica of the old spot, but as something bolder.

The new Tamba is opulent and architecturally deliberate. Art Deco details evoke 1930s Mumbai. The menu, led by Executive Chef Anand Singh — born in the Himalayan foothills of Uttarakhand, trained across six countries — combines traditional Indian cooking with modern live-fire techniques. A tandoor shares the line with a Josper charcoal oven. Coastal-inspired dishes sit alongside Himalayan preparations. The dining room, which seats more than 120, is designed to feel like an event, not just a meal.

The gamble paid off faster than anyone expected.

## A James Beard Finalist in Year One

In March 2026, the James Beard Foundation named Tamba a finalist for Best New Restaurant — one of the most competitive and prestigious categories in America's culinary awards. The nomination came in the restaurant's first year of existence, an extraordinarily rare achievement. Tamba was the only Indian restaurant in the category.

The broader 2026 James Beard cycle marked a watershed moment for Indian and South Asian cuisine in America. In the Outstanding Restaurateur category, both Srijith Gopinathan and Ayesha Thapar of California's Cal-India Collective (operating Ettan, Copra, Eylan, and Little Blue Door across the Bay Area) and Meherwan and Molly Irani of the Chai Pani Restaurant Group were finalists. In the Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic race, Suresh Sundas of Washington D.C.'s Tapori became the first Nepali chef ever nominated for a James Beard Award.

While the top prizes ultimately went elsewhere — New York's Lei won Best New Restaurant, and Michael Tusk of San Francisco's Quince took Outstanding Chef at the June 15 ceremony — the unprecedented breadth of Indian and South Asian representation across categories sent a signal that the American culinary establishment can no longer overlook.

"Our industry is an industry of immigrants," said Damian Diaz, who received the foundation's Humanitarian of the Year award. "Immigrants are what make this America great." The words could have been written for the Dhillons.

## What Tamba Means for Indian Dining

For decades, Las Vegas attracted outposts of established restaurant brands — celebrity chef satellites and luxury hotel dining rooms. Tamba's nomination represents something different: a family-owned, immigrant-built Indian restaurant earning recognition on the strength of its food and vision, not a famous name or a hotel lobby address.

"When you look at the types of places nominated this year versus five years ago, we now have way more representation of cuisines that are not Western cooking," noted chef and food personality Andrew Zimmern at the awards ceremony. "There's an ice cream place in New Hampshire that's nominated. Those kinds of places are really important."

The observation applies to Tamba in full: an Indian restaurant in a Las Vegas shopping centre, competing with the fine-dining establishment and holding its own.

## The Diaspora Take

For Indian Americans in Las Vegas — and the millions who visit the city each year — Tamba's James Beard recognition validates what many have long believed: that Indian cuisine belongs at the highest table in American dining. The Dhillon family's journey from a small Monterey restaurant in 1989 to a James Beard finalist in 2026 is an immigrant arc that resonates far beyond the food itself.

Sunny Dhillon did not simply rebuild his parents' restaurant. He reimagined it for a generation that expects Indian cuisine to compete on craft, ambition, and artistry — and he did it in a city built by people who arrived from somewhere else with something to prove.

Tamba, at Town Square Las Vegas, is open for dinner nightly. The copper, it seems, has been purified.
